title: A Geometry Is Its Group: Klein from the Bonn Physics Bench to the Surface With No Inside
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rhineland and the Physics Bench

stops.name: Jägerhofstraße 11, Düsseldorf, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor, en and de Wikipedia, and Royal Society catalogue NA5396 agree on 25 April 1849, and de.wikipedia gives the street address. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 51.228, 6.784, which is about 280 m off the address. The father's name is Caspar Klein, not the pool's 'Peter Caspar'; 'second of four children' is corroborated by nothing consulted and is not asserted.
stops.campa: Felix Christian Klein is born at Jägerhofstraße 11 in Düsseldorf, in the Rhine Province of Prussia, to Caspar Klein, a Landrentmeister in the provincial administration, and Sophie Elise Kayser. The Rhineland is one year out of the risings of 1848, and its Prussian officials are hated men in a hated uniform. A Royal Society obituary written seventy-nine years later will put cannon on the barricades outside the window that night, with the household packed for flight. The register gives only the date.
stops.quote: Without, the cannon thundered on the barricades raised by the insurgent Rhinelanders against their hated Prussian rulers. Within, although all had been prepared for flight, there was no thought of departure; on that night was born a son to the stern Prussian secretary. That son was Felix Klein.
stops.quote_source: W. H. Young, obituary notice for Felix Klein, Proceedings of the Royal Society A (1928), as quoted on MacTutor
suggested_refs: The house at Jägerhofstraße 11, Düsseldorf, named as the birthplace by de.wikipedia

stops.name: Königliches Gymnasium, Düsseldorf, eight years of Latin and Greek
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1857 by de.wikipedia, which also records the private elementary schooling before it; day and month not recorded, defaulted to 10-01 for the autumn term. The research pool had this tagged as tradition only, which was too weak. The Abitur year 1865 is attested; the pool's 'August 1865' appears in no source consulted and is not used. Coordinates approximate the Altstadt school district, the surviving building not being independently pinned.
stops.campa: After a private elementary school and lessons from his mother, the boy enters the Royal Gymnasium in Düsseldorf and stays eight years. The curriculum is Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and mathematics, in that order of institutional dignity. He takes his Abitur in 1865, sixteen years old, and leaves for Bonn meaning to become a physicist. Of the eight years themselves the record keeps the dates and the syllabus and very little else: no anecdote, no teacher's name, no report of what he was like in a room full of boys.
suggested_refs: The Königliche Gymnasium Düsseldorf, entered autumn 1857

stops.name: Bonn, matriculation in the Kurfürstliches Schloss
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1865 by MacTutor and de.wikipedia; the research pool's exact day, 5 October 1865, is in no source consulted and is not asserted, the date here being the autumn-term default. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 50.7346, 7.0982, which is about 260 m from the university's main building.
stops.campa: Klein matriculates at the University of Bonn, in the old electoral palace, to read mathematics and the natural sciences. He is sixteen. The plan is physics: instruments, laboratory work, measurement. Bonn has Julius Plücker, who holds the chairs of mathematics and experimental physics at once and has lately gone back to the line geometry he put down twenty years before. In the physics rooms Plücker is building discharge tubes with his own hands and watching what the current does inside the glass.
suggested_refs: The Kurfürstliches Schloss, main building of the University of Bonn

stops.name: Poppelsdorf, assistant in experimental physics
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1866 by MacTutor; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates approximate the Poppelsdorf physics institute site; no source consulted pins Plücker's laboratory to a single address.
stops.campa: Plücker takes the seventeen-year-old on as his assistant in experimental physics. Klein sets up apparatus, watches discharges in evacuated glass, and learns a laboratory discipline he never afterward puts down; the plaster surfaces and string models of his later institutes begin here, at a bench, with his hands. In the same rooms Plücker talks line geometry, the coordinate system in which the line and not the point is the primitive element of space. The assistantship runs from 1866 until Plücker dies.
suggested_refs: Julius Plücker, Neue Geometrie des Raumes gegründet auf die Betrachtung der geraden Linie als Raumelement (1868-69)

stops.name: Bonn, Plücker dead and the doctorate finished
stops.date_confidence: Plücker's death on 22 May 1868 and the doctorate in 1868 are both attested by MacTutor; the exact defence date of 12 December 1868, carried by the research pool, is in no source consulted, and the December here orders the segment only. Supervision is contested and the campa says so: MacTutor and en.wikipedia name Plücker, de.wikipedia has Klein studying under Lipschitz and Plücker and promoted under Plücker, and the pool's 'Lipschitz's formal supervision' comes from Tobies alone.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of May Plücker dies with the second volume of his line geometry unfinished, and the work falls to a nineteen-year-old assistant. Klein finishes it. In the same year he defends his own dissertation at Bonn, on the transformation of the general second-degree equation in line coordinates, and takes the highest grade. Who formally presided over that defence the sources answer three different ways: MacTutor names Plücker, who was dead; de.wikipedia has him taught by Lipschitz and promoted under Plücker; Tobies puts Lipschitz in the chair.
suggested_refs: Klein's 1868 Bonn dissertation on the transformation of the general second-degree equation in line coordinates

segments.name: Clebsch, Berlin, Paris, and the War

stops.name: Göttingen, to Alfred Clebsch
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1869 by MacTutor; the research pool's 'January' is unsourced, and 01-01 is the unknown-month default. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin, inherited byte-identical from heisenberg.journey.json and gauss.journey.json. Noted as a standing corpus contradiction: john_von_neumann.journey.json calls a different point, 51.5413, 9.9158, canonical for the same town.
stops.campa: Klein goes to Göttingen to work with Alfred Clebsch and finds there a way of doing mathematics that is also a way of organizing it. Clebsch runs Mathematische Annalen, gathers a school around himself, and hunts connections between fields the specialists keep apart: algebraic geometry, invariant theory, Abelian functions. Klein takes the method and the ambition together, and everything he later builds, the journals and the seminars and the institutes and the funding committees, is Clebsch's practice at a scale Clebsch never lived to try. He is twenty. He stays through the year and then goes to Berlin for the winter semester.
stops.quote: Clebsch must be said to belong both to the second and third of these categories, while I should class myself with the third, and also the first.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture I, 'Clebsch', p. 2, on the division of mathematicians into logicians, formalists and intuitionists
suggested_refs: Mathematische Annalen, founded by Clebsch and Carl Neumann in 1868
sources: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Project Gutenberg #36154

stops.name: Berlin, the winter semester among the analysts
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter semester of 1869 that Klein spent in Berlin; de.wikipedia names Kronecker, Kummer and Weierstrass. Correcting the research pool, which named Otto Stolz and Ludwig Kiepert and cited MacTutor for them: MacTutor's Klein page mentions neither man. The meeting with Sophus Lie in Berlin in 1869 is standard in the biographical literature but was not verified in this pass, so it is reconstruction.
stops.campa: The winter semester takes Klein to Berlin, citadel of analytic rigor, where Kummer, Kronecker, and Weierstrass hold the field and a taste for geometric intuition is treated as a habit to be outgrown. Klein does not outgrow it. He works on non-Euclidean geometry and on Cayley's projective metric, disagreeing quietly with nearly everyone in the room, and here, by tradition, he first meets the Norwegian Sophus Lie. Berlin will hold his method against him for the rest of his working life.
stops.quote: [His mind] teemed with ideas and brilliant reflections, but it is true that his work lacks the stern aspects required by mathematical exactitude.
stops.quote_source: Grace Chisholm Young on the Berlin verdict, tribute to Felix Klein, The Times (1925), transcribed by MacTutor
suggested_refs: Grace Chisholm Young's 1925 tribute in The Times, on Berlin's want of appreciation of Klein's type of mind
sources: MacTutor transcription of the 1925 Times obituary of Klein

stops.name: Paris, the season with Sophus Lie
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1870 by MacTutor's Klein and Lie biographies, which record the joint Paris stay, the meetings with Darboux and Jordan, and the notes in the Comptes Rendus; month not recorded, and April orders the segment ahead of the July declaration of war. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identical from claude_levi_strauss.journey.json.
stops.campa: Klein and Lie travel to Paris together and work side by side for a season. Gaston Darboux, Michel Chasles, and Camille Jordan receive them; short notes go into the Comptes Rendus of the Academy; Jordan presses on Lie how much groups of transformations matter for geometry. What will come out of Klein two years later at Erlangen as a definition of what a geometry is, is in the room already, lying about unassembled. Klein is twenty-one, Lie twenty-seven, and neither of them has a chair.
stops.quote: Fortunately, I had the advantage of becoming intimately acquainted with Lie's ideas at a very early period, when they were still, as the chemists say, in the "nascent state," and thus most effective in producing a strong reaction.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture II, 'Sophus Lie', p. 9
suggested_refs: Camille Jordan, Traité des substitutions et des équations algébriques (1870)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Felix Klein' and 'Sophus Lie'

stops.name: The Lorraine front, the medical orderly
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests only a 'short period as a medical orderly, 1870'. The judgement of unfitness for the ranks, the typhus, and the convalescence at his parents' house in Düsseldorf come from Tobies through the dossier and are reconstruction; MacTutor does not mention typhus. Coordinates mark the general Lorraine theatre, since no source consulted names the sector Klein served in. Lie's arrest is stated in the atlas queue entry for him, not independently fetched.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of July France declares war and the Paris season ends inside a week. Lie, walking in France with a notebook of mathematics, is arrested near Fontainebleau as a suspected spy. Klein goes home to a Prussia mobilizing, is judged unfit for the ranks, and volunteers as a medical orderly, serving some weeks near the front in the typhus that always follows armies. He catches it. He is carried back to his parents' house in Düsseldorf and lies there through the autumn, too weak to work.
suggested_refs: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (Springer, 2021), for the typhus and the judgement of unfitness
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Göttingen, the Habilitation and three semesters as Privatdozent
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor gives 'early 1871' for the Privatdozent appointment and en.wikipedia the Habilitation under Clebsch at Göttingen in 1871. The research pool's 'January 1871' is a false precision; 01-01 here is the unknown-month default. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Recovered, Klein habilitates under Clebsch and is made a Privatdozent. Three semesters follow at a rate that alarms his elders: projective and non-Euclidean geometry, cubic surfaces, transformation groups, and the argument that turns Cayley's projective metric into a proof that non-Euclidean geometry is exactly as consistent as Euclid's, since it can be built inside it. He is twenty-two. A Privatdozent draws no salary, only what his hearers pay him at the door.
stops.quote: we are forced to the opinion that our geometrical demonstrations have no absolute objective truth, but are true only for the present state of our knowledge.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture XI, 'The Most Recent Researches in Non-Euclidean Geometry', p. 93
suggested_refs: Klein's papers of 1871-73 on the so-called non-Euclidean geometry, Mathematische Annalen

segments.name: Erlangen: A Geometry Is Its Group

stops.name: Erlangen, the chair at twenty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1872 by MacTutor and Royal Society catalogue NA5396; month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01, though de.wikipedia dates the call to the winter semester 1872/73. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 49.5947, 11.0086, which is about 450 m from Schloss Erlangen, the university's main building.
stops.campa: On Clebsch's recommendation the University of Erlangen makes Klein a full professor. He is twenty-three, younger than some of the men who will sit in the seminar he founds at once, and he arrives into a small faculty in a small Bavarian town where the historian Karl Hegel also holds a chair. The appointment is an older man's bet on a young one, and Clebsch has fourteen months to live. Before anything else Klein sits down to write the document a new professor owes the faculty on entering it.
suggested_refs: Schloss Erlangen, main building of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität

stops.name: Erlangen, the accession document
stops.date_confidence: the document, its title and the year 1872 are attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. The month is not: 'October 1872' comes from Tobies alone through the dossier, and de.wikipedia dates the Erlangen call to the winter semester 1872/73. October is kept here to order the segment against the December lecture and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: The document is called Vergleichende Betrachtungen über neuere geometrische Forschungen, and it puts a century inside one sentence. A geometry is a space together with a group of transformations, and its content is whatever the group leaves unchanged. Euclidean, affine, projective, non-Euclidean geometry stop being rival subjects and become cases of one procedure, sorted by their groups. Almost nobody reads it for twenty years. Then everybody does, and calls it the Erlangen Program.
stops.quote: every system of geometry is characterized by its group, in the meaning explained in my Erlangen Programm.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture II, p. 11, looking back on the 1872 document twenty-one years later
suggested_refs: Vergleichende Betrachtungen über neuere geometrische Forschungen (Erlangen: Deichert, 1872), translated by M. W. Haskell, Bulletin of the New York Mathematical Society 2 (1893), pp. 215-249

stops.name: Göttingen, the death of Clebsch
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1872 by MacTutor; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Klein's own entry to the editorial board of Mathematische Annalen is dated 1876-1924 by de.wikipedia, which is what the campa's 'within four years' rests on; the research pool's claim of 1873, and of Paul Gordan joining with him, is supported by no source consulted. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Alfred Clebsch dies at Göttingen in November, thirty-nine years old, six months after putting Klein into a chair. Mathematische Annalen loses its founder, the Göttingen school its centre, and the young professor at Erlangen, in the fifth month of his first chair, the only patron he has. Within four years Klein is on the journal's board, and he keeps the seat until 1924, forty-eight years of it. Within fourteen years he holds a chair at Clebsch's own university.
suggested_refs: Mathematische Annalen, whose editorship Klein held from 1876 to 1924

stops.name: Erlangen, the lecture he actually gave
stops.date_confidence: the distinction is attested: MacTutor states that the Erlanger Programm was written for the occasion of the inaugural address 'although it was not actually the speech he gave.' The date of 7 December 1872 and the delivered lecture's subject matter come from Tobies through the dossier and appear in no source consulted; both are reconstruction, and the day is kept only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The Erlangen Program was written for the occasion of the inaugural address. It was not the address. What Klein stands up and delivers to the assembled faculty is a talk about teaching: exercises, seminars, physical models, the training of the men who will teach in the Gymnasien, how mathematics ought to reach the people learning it. Popular biography has fused the two documents ever since. Which of the two the faculty in the room that afternoon believed they had come to hear, no record consulted says.
suggested_refs: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (Springer, 2021), for the content and date of the delivered inaugural lecture
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: London, the crossing to the British
stops.date_confidence: the 1873 British journey comes from Tobies through the dossier and is reconstruction; no source consulted names a city or an institution, so London stands as an acknowledged placeholder rather than a located stop, and 01-01 is the unknown-month default. The 1875 honorary membership of the London Mathematical Society and the later Royal Society honours are attested by MacTutor and catalogue NA5396.
stops.campa: Klein crosses to Britain to meet British mathematicians face to face, at a moment when official Prussian science treats the Channel as a wider water than it is. Arthur Cayley's projective metric is already load-bearing inside his own work on non-Euclidean geometry, and the Annalen wants foreign authors. In 1875 the London Mathematical Society elects him an honorary member. The British connection will hold for forty years, through a Royal Society fellowship and two of its medals.
suggested_refs: The London Mathematical Society's roll of honorary members, which admitted Klein in 1875
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Erlangen, the marriage to Anna Hegel
stops.date_confidence: the year and the relationship are attested by MacTutor, en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia; the research pool's exact day of 17 August 1875 is in no source consulted, and 01-01 is the unknown-month default. The city is unresolved and deliberately left so: encyclopedia.com said Munich but that page now redirects to a 404, while Karl Hegel's chair was at Erlangen, which is why the stop is pinned here. Correcting the pool's geography lens, Anna was Hegel's granddaughter, not his great-granddaughter.
stops.campa: Klein marries Anna Hegel, daughter of the Erlangen historian Karl Hegel and granddaughter of the philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. Where the wedding took place the sources cannot agree: one account puts it at Munich, where Klein has just taken a chair, while the bride's family is at Erlangen. Neither the day nor the church is fixed by anything consulted. He is twenty-six. Four children follow, and the marriage lasts the remaining fifty years of his life.
stops.quote: the sunny days when the tall, handsome young professor wooed and won the lovely granddaughter of the philosopher Hegel.
stops.quote_source: Grace Chisholm Young, tribute to Felix Klein, The Times (1925), transcribed by MacTutor; in the original the clause is attached to the 1872 Erlangen Programme, not to the wedding
suggested_refs: Karl Hegel's professorship at Erlangen, the household into which Klein married
sources: MacTutor transcription of the 1925 Times obituary of Klein

stops.name: Munich, the workshop for surfaces
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1875 by MacTutor, de.wikipedia and Royal Society catalogue NA5396, which gives 'Professor of Mathematics, Munich 1875-1880'. The research pool's exact day of 1 April 1875 is in no source consulted; April is kept to order the segment against the marriage. The reorganisation into a Technische Hochschule in 1877 is attested.
stops.campa: Klein takes the chair at the Munich Polytechnical School, reorganized two years later as a Technische Hochschule, and with Alexander Brill builds a thing German universities do not have: a mathematical institute with a workshop attached. Surfaces that had lived only inside equations get cast in plaster and strung in thread across wire frames, then set on tables where engineering students can walk around them and put a hand on them. The Brill and Schilling catalogues sell the models to universities across Europe for the next forty years.
stops.quote: the naïve intuition is not exact, while the refined intuition is not properly intuition at all, but arises through the logical development from axioms considered as perfectly exact.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture VI, p. 42
suggested_refs: The Brill and Schilling collections of mathematical models, produced from the Munich workshop and sold to universities across Europe

stops.name: Padua, the Italian geometers
stops.date_confidence: both Italian journeys, of 1874 and 1878, come from Tobies through the dossier and are reconstruction; no source consulted fixes either itinerary city by city. Padua is used because Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro worked there, and the coordinate is a plausible node rather than a documented stop. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A second Italian journey, four years after the first, carries Klein among the geometers of the peninsula, Luigi Bianchi at Pisa and Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro at Padua, whose absolute differential calculus will be the working language of general relativity forty years on. Klein is recruiting: for Mathematische Annalen, for a German mathematical orbit, for a network of correspondents that does not yet have a name. Which towns he actually passed through in that year, no source consulted records.
suggested_refs: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (Springer, 2021), for the Italian journeys of 1874 and 1878
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

segments.name: Leipzig: The Quartic, the Bottle, the Collapse

stops.name: Leipzig, the chair of geometry
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1880 by MacTutor and Royal Society catalogue NA5396, which gives 'Leipzig 1880-1886'; the month is unsourced and October orders the academic year. Adolph Mayer's mediation comes from Tobies through the dossier and is reconstruction; Mayer is not named on MacTutor's Klein page. The founding of the Mathematisches Seminar in 1881 was tagged as reconstruction in the research pool and is kept as such.
stops.campa: Leipzig calls Klein to the chair of geometry, by Adolph Mayer's mediation if his biographer is right; no other source consulted names Mayer. He is thirty-one and arrives with a programme: a Mathematisches Seminar, founded the following year, and a school built around the function theory of Bernhard Riemann, which Berlin regards as insufficiently rigorous and Klein regards as the living heart of the subject, geometry and analysis and physics in one apparatus. Leipzig gives him six years.
suggested_refs: The Leipzig Mathematisches Seminar, founded 1881
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Leipzig, the quartic and the surface with no inside
stops.date_confidence: the quartic work of 1878-80 and the bottle of 1882 are attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. One stop carries both because the quartic was begun at Munich and finished at Leipzig, and staging it at a chair Klein did not yet hold would be worse. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The Fläche-to-Flasche mistranslation story is conjecture: Linda Hall Library labels it so, and Göttingen's own model-collection page refused connection in this pass.
stops.campa: Out of the group PSL(2,7) and the curve x cubed y plus y cubed z plus z cubed x equals zero, work begun at Munich and finished here, comes the genus-three surface that carries his name, with one hundred and sixty-eight automorphisms, the most any curve of that genus can have. In the same years he describes a closed surface with no inside and no outside, which cannot sit in three dimensions without passing through itself. In German it is a Fläche, a surface. It reaches English as a bottle.
suggested_refs: Klein, 'Über die Transformation siebenter Ordnung der elliptischen Funktionen', Mathematische Annalen 14 (1878), on the quartic
sources: Linda Hall Library, 'Felix Klein', Scientist of the Day

stops.name: Leipzig, the race with Poincaré and the collapse
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1882 by MacTutor, en.wikipedia and encyclopedia.com, which also carry the prolonged depression of 1883-84; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. The sources describe depression and offer no clinical diagnosis, and none is inferred here.
stops.campa: Klein and Henri Poincaré are racing each other by post toward a general uniformization theorem for algebraic curves, each reading the other's letters, each driving himself further than he can go. Klein is also running a seminar, a journal, and an institute. In the autumn of 1882 he breaks down completely, in body and in mind, and the collapse holds through 1883 and into 1884. He is thirty-three, and the original research of the Leipzig years stops here and does not resume. The sources say depression and name no diagnosis.
suggested_refs: The Klein-Poincaré correspondence of 1881-82 on automorphic functions and uniformization

stops.name: Leipzig, the Baltimore offer refused
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Johns Hopkins approach and the financial grounds for refusing come from Tobies through the dossier, and nothing in MacTutor or either Wikipedia mentions them. The research pool tagged the same event as attested in one lens and reconstructed in another, and appended a corroboration by MacTutor that does not exist. The stop is pinned at Leipzig, where Klein was, and not at Baltimore, which he never saw.
stops.campa: From Baltimore comes an invitation to succeed James Joseph Sylvester at Johns Hopkins: a university seven years old, built on a Baltimore merchant's money, with the best-funded research mathematics in the United States, and a clean way out of a place where he has just fallen apart. Klein reads the terms and declines, on money, according to his biographer. Nothing else consulted records the offer at all, and no letter of refusal is quoted anywhere. He stays at Leipzig, in the second year of not being able to work.
suggested_refs: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (Springer, 2021), for the Johns Hopkins offer and its refusal
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Leipzig, the icosahedron and the quintic
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1884 by MacTutor; month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The judgement that Klein regarded function theory rather than the Erlangen Program as the summit of his work is a third-party characterisation, verbatim from the Dictionary of Scientific Biography article by Burau and Schoeneberg, and not Klein's own words.
stops.campa: The book on the icosahedron and the solution of equations of the fifth degree appears while he is still convalescing. It takes the symmetry group of a Platonic solid, the quintic that Galois theory forbids solving by radicals, and a road between them through elliptic modular functions. It is among the most admired things he ever wrote, and it belongs to the years in which he could not work. Asked later where his own summit lay, he did not point at this book, or at Erlangen.
stops.quote: Klein considered his work in function theory to be the summit of his work in mathematics.
stops.quote_source: Werner Burau and Bruno Schoeneberg, 'Klein, Christian Felix', Dictionary of Scientific Biography
suggested_refs: Klein, Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder und die Auflösung der Gleichungen vom fünften Grade (Leipzig: Teubner, 1884)
sources: Burau and Schoeneberg, 'Klein, Christian Felix', Dictionary of Scientific Biography

stops.name: Leipzig, the call to Göttingen and Lie's succession
stops.date_confidence: the 1886 Göttingen appointment is attested by MacTutor, en.wikipedia and Royal Society catalogue NA5396; month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The vacancy left by Moritz Abraham Stern's retirement and the opposition of Hermann Amandus Schwarz and Ernst Schering are reconstruction: none of the three is named on MacTutor's Klein page, and en.wikipedia's Stern article gives no retirement date. Lie's succession at Leipzig is attested on MacTutor's Lie biography.
stops.campa: Göttingen calls, over opposition from Hermann Amandus Schwarz and Ernst Schering if the archival account is right, and Klein accepts. On his way out he arranges the Leipzig succession for Sophus Lie, the Norwegian he walked Paris with sixteen years before, now the founder of a whole theory of continuous groups. Some German mathematicians take a foreign appointment badly; Klein's position, held for the rest of his life, is that the mathematics is not German or Norwegian and the institution is a tool. Lie holds the Leipzig chair for twelve years.
stops.quote: To fully understand the mathematical genius of Sophus Lie, one must not turn to the books recently published by him in collaboration with Dr. Engel, but to his earlier memoirs, written during the first years of his scientific career.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture II, 'Sophus Lie', p. 9
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie's Leipzig chair, 1886-1898, arranged on Klein's departure
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Felix Klein' and 'Sophus Lie'

segments.name: Göttingen Rebuilt, and the American Campaign

stops.name: Göttingen, the second chair
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1886 by MacTutor, en.wikipedia and Royal Society catalogue NA5396, which records 'Göttingen 1886-1925'; month not recorded, and April orders the arrival after the call. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin, inherited byte-identical from heisenberg.journey.json and gauss.journey.json, in preference to the rival pin at 51.5413, 9.9158 that john_von_neumann.journey.json also calls canonical.
stops.campa: Klein arrives at a Göttingen coasting on a reputation earned by dead men. He is thirty-seven and no longer capable of the sustained original work of the Leipzig years, so he turns everything he has toward building: appointments, seminars, a reading room, foreign students, an institute run as a machine for producing mathematicians rather than a hall where a professor talks. What he can no longer produce himself he arranges for other people to produce. He holds this chair thirty-nine years, and calls the students who come through it collaborators.
stops.quote: I have always regarded my students not merely as hearers or pupils, but as collaborators.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture XII, 'The Study of Mathematics at Göttingen', p. 96
suggested_refs: The Göttingen mathematical reading room and seminar library, built up under Klein after 1886

stops.name: Jackson Park, Chicago, the Columbian Exposition
stops.date_confidence: the 1893 American visit is attested by en.wikipedia; the Chicago fair detail comes from Tobies through the dossier. The fair ran from 1 May to 30 October 1893, so an August visit is consistent; the day is not recorded and is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 41.7825, -87.5806 to en.wikipedia's reading of the Jackson Park site, about 800 m away.
stops.campa: With official Prussian permission Klein sails for the World's Columbian Exposition at Jackson Park and the international congress of mathematicians attached to it, part of a deliberate campaign of American contact. The fair is the largest advertisement for industrial modernity yet built, a white plaster city laid over machine halls on the lakefront. A man who has spent twenty years arguing that mathematics belongs next to engineering is well chosen for it. The congress itself is small.
suggested_refs: The International Mathematical Congress held at Chicago, August 1893, in connection with the Columbian Exposition
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Evanston, the twelve lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested: the lectures ran 28 August to 9 September 1893 and were published as The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), reported by Alexander Ziwet and revised by Klein himself, which is the source fetched for this stop through Project Gutenberg #36154. The racial-typology passage is verbatim from Lecture VI, p. 46, of that printed text. Correcting the research dossier, which cited it to p. 42.
stops.campa: At Northwestern Klein delivers twelve lectures across twelve days, in English, later printed as the Evanston Colloquium: Clebsch, Lie, function theory, non-Euclidean geometry, the working method of Göttingen. It is a recruitment campaign conducted as a survey course, and it works. In the sixth lecture he divides mathematical temperament by race, assigning naive space-intuition to the Teutonic and critical logic to the Latin and Hebrew, and invokes Galton on heredity. He says it in his own English, and it stands in the book.
stops.quote: It would seem as if a strong naïve space-intuition were an attribute pre-eminently of the Teutonic race, while the critical, purely logical sense is more fully developed in the Latin and Hebrew races.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture VI, p. 46
suggested_refs: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium: Lectures on Mathematics, reported by Alexander Ziwet (New York: Macmillan, 1894)
sources: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Project Gutenberg #36154

stops.name: Göttingen, Grace Chisholm's doctorate
stops.date_confidence: the 1895 doctorate under Klein, on algebraic group theory applied to spherical trigonometry, is attested by en.wikipedia and MacTutor's page for Grace Chisholm Young; month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01, the research pool's 'April' being unsourced. The grade magna cum laude and the claim of a first for a woman in Prussia are stated by neither source and are reconstruction. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Grace Chisholm, English, has been admitted to Klein's lectures at a time when Prussian universities do not matriculate women and each professor decides on his own authority whether one may sit in the room. Klein lets her in, supervises the thesis, and in 1895 she takes a Göttingen doctorate in algebraic group theory applied to spherical trigonometry. Whether it is the first such degree given to a woman in Prussia depends on how one counts Kovalevskaya's 1874 degree in absentia. Chisholm sat the examinations.
suggested_refs: Grace Chisholm, Algebraisch-gruppentheoretische Untersuchungen zur sphärischen Trigonometrie (Göttingen, 1895)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Grace Chisholm Young'

stops.name: Weender Chaussee 6, Göttingen, and the second Atlantic crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested: Royal Society catalogue NA5396 lists Klein's address as Weender Chaussee 6, Göttingen, in 1896, and en.wikipedia records a second American visit that year. No itinerary city is confirmed for the trip, which is why the research pool's Washington placeholder pin has been dropped and the crossing folded into this stop rather than given a coordinate it does not have. Coordinate corrected to Weender Landstraße 6, the street's modern name.
stops.campa: Royal Society correspondence gives Klein's address this year as Weender Chaussee 6, Göttingen. From this house he runs an institute that has begun pulling students out of Britain, America, Russia, and Japan, and this year he crosses the Atlantic a second time. He comes home with American practice as a lever to use on Prussian ministries: women in universities, teacher training, industry paying for laboratories. Where in America he went, no source consulted records. He is forty-seven years old.
suggested_refs: Royal Society archive catalogue NA5396, listing Weender Chaussee 6 as Klein's address in 1896

stops.name: Göttingen, the Vereinigung and the manufacturers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1898 by de.wikipedia, which calls the Göttinger Vereinigung the first organisation in Germany to bind industry to a university; the research pool's exact date of 28 February 1898 comes from Tobies alone and is not used, 01-01 being the unknown-month default. The count of some fifty patrons and the naming of Anton von Rieppel are reconstruction. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Klein founds the Göttinger Vereinigung zur Förderung der angewandten Physik, and it is the first body in Germany to bind a university to its industries: manufacturers and engineering firms, Anton von Rieppel among them, paying for institutes, instruments, and new applied chairs. No money goes into a professor's pocket. The mathematicians get buildings and the firms get engineers who can calculate. How many patrons signed on, the record consulted does not settle; the figure of fifty comes from his biographer alone.
suggested_refs: The Göttinger Vereinigung zur Förderung der angewandten Physik und Mathematik, founded 1898
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

segments.name: The School Question, the House of Lords, and the Sanatorium

stops.name: Merano, the reform proposals
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Meran reform proposals of 1905 and the meetings at Stuttgart in 1906 and Dresden in 1907 come from Tobies through the dossier. The Meran proposals are well known in the historiography of mathematics education but were not independently re-fetched in this pass. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At a reform meeting in Merano, Klein's proposals for school mathematics go before the German teaching profession: calculus inside the Gymnasium, functions and graphs taught early, and the whole subject arranged so that schoolroom and university stop being two unrelated countries. Meetings at Stuttgart and Dresden follow over the next two years. He is fifty-six, and he has been making this argument since his first year in a chair. What comes out of Merano is printed as the Meraner Lehrplan.
suggested_refs: The Meraner Lehrplan of 1905, the reform curriculum for German school mathematics
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Wilhelm-Weber-Straße 3, Göttingen, the last house
stops.date_confidence: Royal Society catalogue NA5396 gives this address for 1905 to 1908 only; that he stayed until his death in 1925 is inference beyond the source and is labelled here as such. The wheelchair of the later years comes from Tobies through the dossier and is reconstruction. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 51.533, 9.928, which is 1.1 km away in the city centre and on no part of this street.
stops.campa: The household moves to Wilhelm-Weber-Straße 3. Royal Society letters carry this address from 1905, and it is where Klein lives out his last twenty years, increasingly confined to a wheelchair, receiving students in a room rather than lecturing to them in a hall. The seminars come to the house. So do the foreign visitors, and in time the proofs of the collected works. The Royal Society record itself only runs to 1908; the rest is inference from the fact that he never moves again.
suggested_refs: Royal Society archive catalogue NA5396, listing Wilhelm-Weber-Straße 3 as Klein's address 1905-1908
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the seat in the House of Lords
stops.date_confidence: the seat as the University of Göttingen's representative in the Preußisches Herrenhaus, and its end with the Empire in 1918, are treated as established; the research pool's appointment date of 17 February 1908 comes from Tobies alone and is not asserted, 01-01 standing as the unknown-month default. Coordinate corrected to the Bundesrat building, Leipziger Straße 3-4, the former Herrenhaus, about 340 m from the pool's pin.
stops.campa: The University of Göttingen sends Klein to the Prussian House of Lords as its representative, a nonpartisan seat in a chamber of princes, landowners, and bishops. He uses it for schools. Primary and secondary curricula, girls' schools, vocational training, teacher education: the whole apparatus underneath the university, argued for from inside the Prussian state by a man who has been arguing for it from outside for thirty-five years. The seat lasts until the Empire that created it falls in 1918.
suggested_refs: The Preußisches Herrenhaus, Leipziger Straße, Berlin, dissolved with the Empire in 1918
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Rome, first president of the commission
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: Klein was chosen as the first president of what became the International Commission on Mathematical Instruction at the 1908 International Congress of Mathematicians in Rome. Tobies dates the presidency 1908-1920, which is reconstruction. Coordinates mark central Rome; the congress venue within the city is not independently confirmed here.
stops.campa: At the fourth International Congress of Mathematicians the delegates create an international commission on mathematical instruction and elect Klein its first president. It is the institutional form of an argument he first made as a new professor at Erlangen, in the lecture that got buried under the Program. He is fifty-nine. The commission's first work is a country-by-country survey of how mathematics is actually taught; Tobies dates the presidency 1908 to 1920, and no other source consulted gives an end year.
suggested_refs: The International Commission on Mathematical Instruction, founded at the Rome congress of 1908
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Felix Klein' and 'International Commission on Mathematical Instruction'

stops.name: Burlington House, London, the Copley Medal
stops.date_confidence: the Copley Medal of 1912, the Royal Society foreign membership of 1885 and the De Morgan Medal of 1893 are attested by MacTutor and Royal Society catalogue NA5396; the honorary Cambridge doctorate of 1897 is reconstruction from standard honours listings. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Whether Klein travelled to London in person to receive the medal is not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The Royal Society gives Klein the Copley Medal, its oldest and highest honour, twenty-seven years after electing him a foreign member and nineteen after the London Mathematical Society gave him its De Morgan Medal; Cambridge had made him an honorary doctor in 1897. Whether he was well enough to come to Burlington House and take it in his hands is not recorded anywhere consulted. Within two years his country is at war with Britain, and every one of those honours is an enemy's.
suggested_refs: Royal Society archive catalogue NA5396, recording the Copley Medal of 1912

stops.name: Göttingen, the sanatorium and the retirement
stops.date_confidence: the 1913 retirement on health grounds is attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia; month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The long sanatorium stay preceding it comes from Tobies through the dossier and is reconstruction, and no source consulted names the sanatorium's location, which is why the stop sits at Göttingen and states the gap rather than inventing a spa town. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Decades of overwork come due, on a constitution that never fully repaired itself after 1882. Klein spends a long stay in a sanatorium, in a place no source consulted names, and retires from the Göttingen chair in 1913, earlier than a full career would run, on grounds of health. Retirement in his case means the lectures move to his house and the committees do not stop. He is sixty-four, and has held chairs at Erlangen, Munich, Leipzig, and Göttingen for forty-one consecutive years.
suggested_refs: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (Springer, 2021), for the sanatorium stay preceding the 1913 retirement
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

segments.name: The Signature, the Home Seminars, and the End

stops.name: Göttingen, An die Kulturwelt!
stops.date_confidence: the manifesto, its date, its content and its signatory list are well documented; Klein's signature reaches this file through Tobies and Cordula Tollmien as the dossier summarises them. Deliberately not asserted: the research pool's claim that the French Académie des Sciences annulled Klein's membership on 15 March 1915. No source consulted records any such annulment, and fr.wikipedia's article on the manifesto records that the Académie des Sciences was the most hesitant of the French academies on exactly this question.
stops.campa: Klein's name appears on An die Kulturwelt!, the manifesto of ninety-three German scientists, writers, and artists denying that Germany caused the war, denying that the violation of Belgian neutrality was a crime, denying the atrocities reported out of Louvain and Dinant. He signs, as most of the ninety-three signed, without seeing a final text. A historian's later reconstruction has him regretting it and opposing reprisals against French colleagues. What he understood on the day is not recoverable. The signature is.
suggested_refs: An die Kulturwelt! Ein Aufruf, October 1914, and Cordula Tollmien's study of the Göttingen signatories
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier
Cordula Tollmien, as summarised in the research dossier

stops.name: Wilhelm-Weber-Straße 3, the seminars in the house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the wartime seminars and historical lectures at Klein's own house, and their becoming the posthumously published Vorlesungen über die Entwicklung der Mathematik im 19. Jahrhundert, come from Tobies through the dossier. That the Vorlesungen open on Gauss is standard description of the book and was not verified in this pass. Date set to 1915 to order the segment inside the war years. Coordinate corrected as at the 1905 residence stop.
stops.campa: With the university emptied of its students and its younger lecturers gone to the front, Klein holds seminars and historical lectures in his own house through the war years. The material becomes the Vorlesungen über die Entwicklung der Mathematik im 19. Jahrhundert, a history of his own century written by a man who was inside most of it. It opens where the century opens, on Gauss, in the town where Gauss spent sixty years. The book is not printed until the year after Klein's death.
suggested_refs: Felix Klein, Vorlesungen über die Entwicklung der Mathematik im 19. Jahrhundert (Springer, 1926-27), assembled from these lectures
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Göttingen, the conservation laws
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1918 papers on Hilbert's foundations of physics and on the differential laws for the conservation of momentum and energy in Einstein's gravitation theory come from Tobies through the dossier, cross-referenced against Klein's own published output of the period. The Klein-Einstein correspondence is well documented in the general literature but was not fetched in this pass, and Klein's part in publicising Noether's theorems is dossier-only. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Retirement does not end the physics. Klein publishes on Hilbert's foundations of physics and on the differential laws for the conservation of momentum and energy in Einstein's theory of gravitation, and writes to Einstein directly about what conservation can even mean once spacetime is itself a variable. In the same Göttingen conversation Emmy Noether proves the theorems that answer the question, and Klein, who has spent thirty years putting other people's work where it can be seen, is one of the men who make sure the physicists hear about hers. He is sixty-nine and has been out of a chair for five years.
suggested_refs: Klein, 'Über die Differentialgesetze für die Erhaltung von Impuls und Energie in der Einsteinschen Gravitationstheorie' (1918)
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Göttingen, the emergency association
stops.date_confidence: the founding of the Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Wissenschaft on 30 October 1920 is attested by de.wikipedia, which names Fritz Haber and Friedrich Schmidt-Ott as its driving figures and does not mention Klein at all. Klein's chairmanship of its committee for mathematics, astronomy and geodesy therefore comes from Tobies alone and is reconstruction. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: German science is broke, the currency is going, and on the thirtieth of October the Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Wissenschaft is founded to keep research alive on emergency money. Klein takes the chair of its committee for mathematics, astronomy, and geodesy, at seventy-one, from a wheelchair. He has been putting money and mathematics in one room since the Vereinigung of 1898. This time the money is the state's rather than industry's, and there is very little of it.
suggested_refs: The Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Wissenschaft, founded 30 October 1920, ancestor of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Göttingen, the collected papers and the self-portrait
stops.date_confidence: the three-volume Gesammelte mathematische Abhandlungen appeared from Springer between 1921 and 1923, which is attested; Klein's own participation in preparing them and the arrangement by domain rather than chronology come from Tobies and are reconstruction, as does the 1923 autobiographical piece in the Mitteilungen des Universitätsbundes Göttingen. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Springer brings out the Gesammelte mathematische Abhandlungen in three volumes, Klein working on them himself, arranging fifty years of papers by domain rather than by date so that the lines of thought stay visible across the decades. In 1923 he writes a short account of his own life for the Göttingen university association's bulletin, one of the Lebensbilder von eigener Hand, portraits drawn by their own subjects. It runs to a few pages, and it is selective, as such things are.
stops.quote: my general aim being to gain, in the course of time, a complete view of the whole field of modern mathematics, with particular regard to the intuitional or (in the highest sense of the term) geometrical standpoint.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, The Evanston Colloquium (Macmillan, 1894), Lecture XII, p. 96
suggested_refs: Felix Klein, Gesammelte mathematische Abhandlungen, 3 vols (Berlin: Springer, 1921-1923)
sources: Renate Tobies, Felix Klein (2021), via the research dossier

stops.name: Wilhelm-Weber-Straße 3, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor, en and de Wikipedia and Royal Society catalogue NA5396 all give 22 June 1925 at Göttingen. Long-standing ill health is documented and no specific terminal cause is established in any source consulted, so none is supplied. Whether the death occurred at this house rather than a clinic is not confirmed; the address is used as his last documented residence, with the coordinate corrected as above.
stops.campa: Felix Klein dies at Göttingen on the twenty-second of June, seventy-six years old. The sources record long declining health and record no terminal cause. He had been a professor for fifty-three years, held four chairs, edited the leading journal of his discipline for nearly half a century, sat in a parliament for a decade, and signed one document he could not take back. The German obituaries call him the most famous German mathematician of his day.
suggested_refs: The 1925 obituaries in The Times and in the Mitteilungen des Universitätsbundes Göttingen

segments.name: After: The Surface With No Inside

stops.name: Stadtfriedhof, Göttingen, the grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the Göttingen Stadtfriedhof is attested by de.wikipedia's Klein article and by its article on the cemetery, which lists him among the notable graves; the burial date itself is not recorded, so the stop carries the death date to keep the segment in order. Coordinate taken from the cemetery article's own reading, 51 degrees 31 minutes 57 seconds north by 9 degrees 54 minutes 35 seconds east, replacing two mutually inconsistent wrong pairs in the research pool. The plot is not fixed by anything consulted.
stops.campa: He is buried at the Stadtfriedhof on the Kasseler Landstraße, at the eastern edge of Grone, the municipal cemetery where Göttingen puts its professors. The burial is attested by the cemetery's own register of notable graves, which lists him; no source consulted gives the date of the funeral, the officiant, or the number of the plot. He first came to the town in 1869, as a student of Clebsch; he came back in 1886, and stayed thirty-nine years without another call.
suggested_refs: The Stadtfriedhof Göttingen, Kasseler Landstraße, and its register of notable graves

stops.name: Göttingen, the papers and the names
stops.date_confidence: posthumous. The Nachlass at the Zentrales Archiv deutscher Mathematiker-Nachlässe in the Göttingen state and university library, the Kaiserslautern centre, the Göttingen Gymnasium and the lecture halls at Düsseldorf and Leipzig are attested by de.wikipedia; minor planet (12045) Klein and the ICMI award by en.wikipedia. The date 1926-01-01 orders the segment and marks no event: no source consulted dates the deposit of the papers or the naming of the buildings. The EMS Felix Klein Prize could not be verified, both pages returning 404.
stops.campa: Klein's papers go to the Zentrales Archiv deutscher Mathematiker-Nachlässe at the Göttingen state and university library, where the protocols of his seminars, kept volume by volume for forty years, stay readable. The name spreads outward from there without him: a lecture hall in the city where he was born, another in the city where he collapsed, a Gymnasium in Göttingen, an applied-mathematics centre at Kaiserslautern, a medal for lifetime work in mathematics teaching, and a minor planet found from Arizona in 1997.
suggested_refs: The Klein Protokolle, the seminar protocols of 1872-1912, held at the Niedersächsische Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Göttingen

stops.name: The Science Museum, London, blown in glass
stops.date_confidence: posthumous, seventy years after Klein's death, and included as the afterlife of his own object rather than as a place he went. Attested by en.wikipedia's Klein bottle article, which records the set made for the Science Museum by the glassblower Alan Bennett in 1995; the museum's own object page returned 404 in this pass. Month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The glassblower Alan Bennett makes a set of Klein bottles for the Science Museum in London, hand-blown variations on a surface that cannot exist in three dimensions. What stands in the case is an immersion and not an embedding: the neck passes through the wall because in this many dimensions it has to, and the true surface, the one with no inside, needs a fourth. Visitors pick the shape up with their eyes and believe they are holding it. Klein described it at Leipzig in 1882 and never drew it as a bottle.
suggested_refs: Alan Bennett's 1995 glass Klein bottles, Science Museum, London
sources: Linda Hall Library, 'Felix Klein', Scientist of the Day
